question: Which great personality of the world was also known as 'Fuehrer'? (RRB JE ME (19/09/2019) Shift 2 CBT 2)
options: Adolf Hitler
Vladimir Lenin
Joseph Stalin
Napoleon Bonaparte
solution:
Solution: Correct Answer is Adolf Hitler

Explanation:
Adolf Hitler (1889-1945) was the dictator of Germany and leader of the Nazi Party, known as 'Führer', a German word meaning 'leader' or 'guide'. He ruled Germany from 1934 to 1945 and was responsible for World War II and the Holocaust. The title 'Führer' signified his absolute dictatorial power. Other options: Vladimir Lenin (Russian revolutionary), Joseph Stalin (Soviet dictator) and Napoleon Bonaparte (French emperor) were not called 'Führer'.

question: When was the Gandhi - Irwin pact carried out? (RRB JE ME (19/09/2019) Shift 2 CBT 2)
options: 1930
1931
1941
1940
solution:
Solution: Correct Answer is 1931

Explanation:
The Gandhi-Irwin Pact was signed on 5 March 1931 between Mahatma Gandhi and the then Viceroy Lord Irwin. This pact was signed before the Second Round Table Conference, in which Gandhi participated. Under this pact, the Civil Disobedience Movement was suspended and political prisoners were released. However, the pact failed as Indian demands were not accepted at the Round Table Conference. This pact was a significant phase in the Indian freedom struggle.

question: When was the French East India Company set up? (RRB JE EE (01/09/2019) Shift 1 CBT 2)
options: 1665
1667
1664
1666
solution:
Solution: Correct Answer is 1664

Explanation:
The French East India Company (Compagnie des Indes Orientales) was established in 1664 during the reign of King Louis XIV of France, under the patronage of his minister Jean-Baptiste Colbert. Its purpose was to trade with India and East Asia and to establish French colonies. The company set up its first factory in Surat in India and later made Pondicherry (in 1673) its main headquarters. The arrival of the French East India Company led to rivalry with the British, eventually resulting in the Carnatic Wars. The company was dissolved in 1769, but it laid the foundation for French influence in India, especially in the southern regions.

question_hi: फ़्रांसीसी ईस्ट इंडिया कंपनी की स्थापना कब हुई थी? (RRB JE EE (01/09/2019) Shift 1 CBT 2)

Explanation:
फ़्रांसीसी ईस्ट इंडिया कंपनी (French East India Company) की स्थापना 1664 में फ्रांस के राजा लुई चौदहवें (लुई XIV) के शासनकाल में उनके मंत्री जीन-बैप्टिस्ट कोलबर्ट ने की थी। इसका उद्देश्य भारत और पूर्वी एशिया के साथ व्यापार करना तथा फ्रांसीसी उपनिवेश स्थापित करना था। कंपनी ने भारत में अपनी पहली फैक्ट्री सूरत में स्थापित की और बाद में पांडिचेरी (1673) को अपना प्रमुख केंद्र बनाया। फ्रांसीसी ईस्ट इंडिया कंपनी का भारत में आगमन अंग्रेजों और फ्रांसीसियों के बीच प्रतिद्वंद्विता का कारण बना, जो बाद में कर्नाटक युद्धों का रूप ले लिया। कंपनी 1769 में भंग हो गई, लेकिन इसने भारत में फ्रांसीसी प्रभाव की नींव रखी।

question: When did Bihar bifurcate from Bengal and some parts of Chota Nagpur merge into Bengal? (RRB JE EE (01/09/2019) Shift 1 CBT 2)
options: 1915
1912
1914
1913
solution:
Solution: Correct Answer is 1912

Explanation:
Bihar was bifurcated from Bengal in 1912 when the British government partitioned the Bengal Presidency to create the new province of Bihar and Orissa. During this process, some parts of Chota Nagpur were merged into Bengal. This bifurcation followed the annulment of the 1905 partition of Bengal in 1911. Under the 1912 reforms, Bihar and Orissa were made a separate province, while certain areas of Chota Nagpur remained part of Bengal. Later, in 1936, Orissa was separated as a distinct province.

question: Which of the following chronological order of events of the freedom struggle is correct? (RRB NTPC CBT-I (10/02/2021) Shift 1)
options: Non cooperative movement – Sepoy mutiny – Champaran movement – Partition of Bengal

Non cooperative movement - Champaran movement - Partition of Bengal - Sepoy mutiny
Non cooperative movement - Champaran movement - Sepoy mutiny - Partition of Bengal
solution:
Solution: Correct Answer is Sepoy mutiny - Partition of Bengal - Champaran movement - Non cooperative movement

Explanation:
The Sepoy Mutiny (1857) was the first major revolt against British rule. This was followed by the Partition of Bengal in 1905 by Lord Curzon, which led to the Swadeshi movement. The Champaran movement (1917) was Mahatma Gandhi's first successful satyagraha against the exploitation of indigo farmers. The Non-Cooperation Movement (1920-22) was a mass movement launched by Gandhi urging non-cooperation with the British. This is the correct chronological order.

question: Which among the following was one of the conceivers of the Kakori robbery? (RRB NTPC CBT-I (10/02/2021) Shift 2)
options: Sukhdev
Bhagat Singh
Udham Singh
Ashfaqullah Khan
solution:
Solution: Correct Answer is Ashfaqullah Khan

Explanation:
The Kakori Train Action (9 August 1925) was executed by the Hindustan Republican Association (HRA). It was conceived by Ram Prasad Bismil, Ashfaqullah Khan, and Chandrashekhar Azad. The objective was to loot the government treasury to fund revolutionary activities. Bismil and Ashfaqullah were later hanged, while Azad died in a police encounter. Sukhdev, Bhagat Singh, and Udham Singh were not involved in this plan. Bhagat Singh joined HRA later but did not participate in Kakori. Sukhdev also joined HRA subsequently. Udham Singh is associated with the Jallianwala Bagh massacre.

question: Subsidiary Alliance, through which the British were responsible for protecting their Indian allies from external and internal threats to their power, was devised by: (RRB NTPC CBT-I (11/02/2021) Shift 1)
options: Lord Dalhousie
Lord Curzon
Lord Wellesley
Lord Bentinck
solution:
Solution: Correct Answer is Lord Wellesley

Explanation:
The Subsidiary Alliance system was devised by Lord Wellesley (Governor-General from 1798 to 1805). Under this system, Indian states had to disband their own armies and pay for British military protection. In return, the British pledged to protect them from external and internal threats. This effectively ended the sovereignty of Indian states and brought them under British control. The first subsidiary alliance was signed with the Nizam of Hyderabad in 1798. Later, states like Mysore, Tanjore, and Awadh also accepted this alliance. Lord Wellesley used this policy to expand British influence in India without direct war.

question: When did the British Cabinet Mission arrive in India in order to examine the Muslim League's demand, and to suggest a suitable political framework for a free India? (RRB NTPC CBT-I (11/02/2021) Shift 2)

question: Prior to which of the following events was the Gandhi-Irwin Pact signed? (RRB NTPC CBT-I (12/02/2021) Shift 1)

Second Round Table Conference
First Round Table Conference
solution:

Explanation:
The Gandhi-Irwin Pact was signed on 5 March 1931. As per the pact, the Civil Disobedience Movement was withdrawn, political prisoners were released, and salt tax was discussed. After the pact, Mahatma Gandhi attended the Second Round Table Conference (September-December 1931, London) as the sole representative of the Indian National Congress. The conference failed due to disagreements on minority issues. The First Round Table Conference (1930-31) was held without Congress participation, and the Third Round Table Conference (1932) was held in Gandhi's absence. The Lucknow Session of Congress (1916) was before the pact but is not the correct answer as it is not a Round Table Conference. Thus, the Gandhi-Irwin Pact was signed prior to the Second Round Table Conference.

question: Who introduced the Vernacular Press Act in India? (RRB NTPC CBT-I (04/03/2021) Shift 1)
options: Lord Willingdon
Lord Lytton
Lord Dalhousie
Lord Ripon
solution:
Solution: Correct Answer is Lord Lytton

Explanation:
The Vernacular Press Act was introduced in India in 1878 by Lord Lytton (full name Robert Lytton). This act was designed to impose strict control on Indian language newspapers. Its aim was to suppress the spirit of the independence movement and prevent critical writing against the government. Lord Lytton served as Viceroy of India, and this act is often referred to as the 'gagging act' because it curbed press freedom. Under this law, any vernacular newspaper could be seized without trial. Later, in 1882, Lord Ripon repealed this act.
